column4: The section's root ه د ي describes leading along a way; Moses answers that the Lord gives each thing its form and then guides it, bringing the section's creation-and-guidance sequence into one formulation.
The section names root ه د ي for a guide who goes ahead; this ayah asks whether the one who guides to truth is more worthy to follow than one who cannot find the way without being guided.
The section explicitly names root ي س ر for ease and preparation; 92:7 applies the same easing verb to the one who gives, fears, and confirms, making ease the outcome of a chosen course.
The section's root ي س ر names ease; here the same verb carries the miserly denier toward hardship, reversing 92:7 and showing that the mount image has two destinations.
The section names root ي س ر for making something easy; this ayah says God made the human way easy, turning the section's passenger-and-route image into a direct statement about human life.
The section names root ه د ي for showing a way; this ayah says the path was shown and leaves the traveler grateful or ungrateful, matching the image's guided route and differing responses.
The section names root ش ق و for hardship; this ayah promises that whoever follows God's guidance will neither stray nor become wretched, directly linking the right route to release from misery.

The section's worst traveler keeps the reminder aside; this ayah gives that turning away its own consequence, a constricted life and gathering blind, completing 20:123's promise about following guidance.
The section names root ش ق و for hardship; God tells Muhammad that the Qur'an was not sent down to make him wretched, a direct boundary on the section's promise of ease.
The section pairs ease for the Prophet with a reminder for the one who fears; this neighboring ayah says the Qur'an is a reminder for the God-fearing, specifying the purpose after 20:2.
The section names root ي س ر for ease; Moses asks God to make his task easy, a second prophetic request that places ease inside an undertaking.
The section names root ش ق و for hardship; God warns Adam that expulsion from the garden would leave him struggling, giving misery a concrete life-and-provision setting.
The section says hardship and ease can accompany one another; this ayah states that with hardship comes ease, directly articulating that relation.
The section cites the hardship-and-ease pairing; this adjacent ayah repeats the ease promise, giving the pairing a second, emphatic statement.
The section names root ي س ر for ease and contrasts it with difficulty; this ayah says God wants ease for people and does not want hardship, in a concrete rule about fasting.
The section joins fear of God with remembrance and ease; here the one who fears God is promised that God will make his affair easy, joining the same stance to ease.
The section names root ه د ي for guidance; this oath-surah states that guidance is God's responsibility, placing the route's leading hand with the same speaker who eases it.
The section recalls the two heights and the hard ascent; this ayah says God guided the human to two high ways, making the route imagery explicit.
The section cites the ascent that the traveler does not attempt; this ayah names the refusal itself, and 90:12–17 explain what that difficult pass entails.
The section names root ج ن ب for keeping something away and shows the wretched person keeping the reminder aside; Abraham instead asks God to keep him and his sons away from idol worship.

The section names root ج ن ب for avoidance; this ayah praises those who use that same root to keep away from false gods and turn toward God, clarifying that avoidance can protect rather than reject guidance.
The section's dictionary form سَوَاءٌ names a middle or level place; this ayah places a companion in the middle of Hell, turning the middle-place image into the road's wrong end.

The section explicitly gives the dictionary form استوى على ظهر دابته for mounting and settling on an animal's back; this ayah uses that very riding-and-settling scene and adds remembrance of God's gift.
The section's dictionary form يَسْرٌ means easy to guide and quick to follow; this ayah calls the earth docile, tells people to walk its slopes, and points from provision to return to God.

The section pictures an easy mount carrying its rider along a route; this ayah says livestock carry loads to distant lands people could not reach without hardship, making the mount's easing function concrete.
The section names root ه د ي for showing the route; this ayah says God directs the way while some routes are crooked, making guidance and deviation two actual directions.
The section develops a mountain ascent and a road that can be guided; this ayah places paths among mountains and rivers so people may find their way.
The section says the road may be one while the traveler's response differs; this ayah commands following one straight path and warns against side paths that divide people from it.
The section's root ه د ي describes showing the way; the opening prayer asks God to guide its speaker onto the straight path, making guidance a request from the traveler.
The section says the wretched person turns aside from the reminder; this ayah asks why people are turning away from it, naming the same refusal before portraying it as animal flight.
The section's dictionary note describes a calm, well-guided walk rather than a defeated rush; this ayah compares the reminder's avoiders to startled wild donkeys, making the opposite gait visible.
The section's calm movement contrasts with a fleeing traveler; this ayah completes 74:50 by saying the donkeys flee from a pursuer, showing avoidance as flight.
The section's 87:9–11 sequence commands remembrance, then distinguishes the fearful rememberer from the one who avoids it; this ayah likewise commands the Prophet to remind.
The section presents a reminder that benefits some hearers; this neighboring ayah limits the Prophet's role to reminding, clarifying the command in 88:21.
The section's worst person avoids the reminder; this ayah identifies the one who turns away and disbelieves as the exception to the reminder's audience.
The section sends its avoider toward the great Fire; this ayah supplies the punishment for the turner-away named in 88:23.
The section links avoiding the reminder with preferring worldly life; this ayah describes someone who turns away from God's remembrance and wants only the life of this world.
The section contrasts the fearful rememberer with the wretched avoider; this passage begins its paired destinies with the one who transgresses, setting up the worldly preference in 79:38.
The section says people prefer the nearer worldly life; this ayah names that preference as the defining choice of the transgressor before giving his destination in 79:39.
The section's avoider reaches the great Fire; this ayah names Hell as the transgressor's destination, completing the worldly preference described in 79:38.
The section says the one who fears remembers; this ayah describes one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire, the opposite course to 79:38.
The section gives the Fire as the wrong destination; this ayah names the Garden as the destination of the one who feared and restrained desire in 79:40.
The section names root س و ي in 87:2 for fashioning; this oath describes the soul as fashioned, using the same root in the same sense and making the fashioned creature the subject of the next choice.
The section's road separates travelers by how they proceed; this ayah says the soul was inspired with its wickedness and piety, specifying the opposed directions behind 91:9–10.
The section's wider surah says the successful one purifies himself; this ayah likewise calls successful the one who purifies the soul, making the right course's result explicit.
The section sets the successful purified person against the wretched avoider; this ayah gives the opposite outcome to the soul buried in corruption.
The section's full surah ends its wrong road in a Fire where one neither dies nor lives; this ayah gives that same boundary to the criminal who comes to his Lord.
The section's 87:9–10 passage commands a reminder that the fearful will remember; this ayah calls the revelation itself a reminder.
The section says the fearful will remember; this neighboring ayah says whoever wills may remember, specifying a hearer's response to the reminder in 80:11.
The section names root ي س ر for ease and then turns to remembrance; this ayah says the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance, joining those two details directly.
The section joins ease to the call to remember; this ayah repeats that the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance, renewing the same invitation in its own passage.
The section joins ease to the call to remember; this ayah repeats the Qur'an's ease for remembrance in a third passage.
The section joins ease to the call to remember; this ayah repeats the same ease-for-remembrance refrain in a fourth passage.
The section names root ي س ر for making the Prophet's task easy and pairs it with reminding; this ayah says the Qur'an was made easy on Muhammad's tongue to warn and give good news.
The section names root ي س ر and then commands a reminder; this ayah says the revelation was made easy on the Prophet's tongue so people may remember.
The section's dictionary form سَوَاءٌ names an even middle; this ayah says one who exchanges faith for disbelief has lost the سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ, joining the middle-place sense to a lost road.
The section names root ه د ي for the guide who leads ahead; this ayah reverses that role by commanding wrongdoers to be led to the path of Hell.
The section names root ه د ي for guidance and develops walking; this ayah contrasts one who walks fallen on his face with one who walks upright on a straight path.
The section treats the route as a way God makes accessible; this ayah says God made paths through the earth for people, connecting creation with passage.
The section names root ه د ي for showing the way; this ayah says God made paths through the earth so people may be guided.
The section places a hard ascent on the route; this ayah describes mountains and broad paths laid through them, a physical setting for guided passage.
The section uses 92:7 to show ease for the giver; this ayah identifies the first traveler as one who gives and fears, supplying the conduct that precedes that ease.
The section contrasts 92:7 with ease for the giver; this ayah adds that he confirms the good promise, completing the description of the traveler before the outcome.
The section uses 92:10 for the hard outcome; this ayah identifies the contrasting traveler as miserly and self-sufficient, the conduct that precedes it.
The section's hard route in 92:10 follows a refusal; this ayah says the miserly traveler denies the good promise, specifying what 92:10 follows.
The section's 87:2–3 sequence moves from creation and measure to guidance; this ayah says the human was created and determined, setting up 80:20's eased path.
The section cites the unattempted ascent in 90:11; this ayah asks what the steep pass is, introducing the actions that verses 13–17 name.
The section's image makes a difficult ascent matter; this ayah defines its first step as freeing a neck, giving the pass a concrete ethical cost.
The section names an ascent not attempted; this ayah says its next step is feeding on a day of hunger, specifying another part of the climb.
The section names a difficult pass; this ayah locates its feeding duty in care for an orphan who is near.
The section names a difficult pass; this ayah extends its food duty to a poor person in misery.
The section contrasts those who follow guidance with the wretched who turn away; this ayah completes the pass's acts with belief, urging patience and mercy among one another.
The section makes the route depend on how the traveler proceeds; this ayah calls those who take the pass's way companions of the right.
The section gives a wrong destination for the one who refuses; this ayah contrasts the companions of the right with those who reject God's signs.
The section's wrong road ends in Fire; this ayah closes the opposing road with fire locked around its travelers.
The section cites Abraham's request to be kept away from idols; this neighboring ayah says idols led many astray and distinguishes those who follow Abraham, explaining his request.
After the section's 37:55 sight of the companion in Hell, the saved speaker says the other nearly ruined him, making their diverging paths explicit.
The section shows one companion in Hell; this ayah says that without his Lord's favor the speaker too would have been brought there, naming the escape that separates their outcomes.
The section develops the mount that carries its rider; this ayah supplies the ships and livestock intended for riding, which 43:13 shows the rider settling upon.
The section describes a journey and its destination; this adjacent ayah says the riders return to their Lord, giving the mounted journey an ultimate direction.
The section's dictionary form يَسْرٌ describes a docile animal that follows readily; this ayah says God subjected livestock to people, some of which they ride.
The section adds a mount to the promise of ease; this ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys as animals for riding, supplying the literal mount scene.
The section pictures an animal bearing its rider along an easy route; this ayah says God made livestock for people to ride and use, grounding the image in provision.
The section develops a mount carrying a passenger; this ayah says people are carried on livestock and ships, completing 40:79's benefits with travel.
The section's passenger is carried on a mount; this ayah says people are carried on livestock and ships, another direct Qur'anic scene of travel by animal.
The section follows a road journey with a mount; this ayah depicts pilgrims arriving on foot and on lean camels from distant passes.
The section's dictionary form هَدْيٌ describes a calm, good manner of walking; this ayah depicts the servants of the Merciful walking gently on earth.
The section's dictionary form هَدْيٌ describes a composed gait; this ayah tells the walker to moderate his pace, giving that secondary walking sense a concrete counterpart.
The section's mount moves easily and its guide walks calmly; this ayah depicts charging animals driving into a gathered host, a forceful mounted movement at the opposite pace.
The section's guided route is distinguished from the wretched road; this ayah names the path of those favored and contrasts it with those who incur anger or stray.
The section's guide goes ahead to show a route; this ayah reverses the role by putting Satan in wait on God's straight path to intercept its travelers.
The section says the same road's travelers differ in how they proceed; this ayah continues Satan's threat to approach people from every direction, showing how the straight path is resisted.
The section joins the reminder to a guided road; this ayah calls the revelation a reminder and says whoever wills may take a path to his Lord.
The section's traveler chooses whether to receive the reminder; this ayah qualifies that human willing remains under God's will.
The section's path ends in ease or the great Fire; this ayah contrasts entry into God's mercy with painful punishment for wrongdoers.
The section's root ه د ي describes being led along a way; this ayah promises guidance to God's ways for those who strive for Him, linking effort on the path with guidance.
The section distinguishes a guided road from turning aside; this ayah accuses people of trying to make God's way crooked and seeking to lead believers from it.
The section's guide points a traveler along a way; this ayah describes people who want others to lose the path, making deliberate misdirection the opposing act.
The section names root ش ق و for hardship and the wretched; this ayah divides people at the final hour into wretched and blessed, framing the outcomes named in 11:106 and 108.
The section names root ش ق و for the wretched traveler who reaches the Fire; this ayah places the wretched in Hell, where they groan and cry out.
The section's wrong road ends in fire; this adjacent ayah gives the opposite end to the blessed, who remain in the Garden.
The section treats a route as passage across created ground; this ayah says God spread the earth out for people, setting up 71:20's broad roads.
The section's traveler follows a route; this ayah says God made broad roads in the spread earth for people to pass along.

The section's dictionary form السَّوِيَّة is a covering placed over a camel's hump; this ayah depicts portable animal-hide dwellings used in travel and at rest, a related but different use of animal covering.
After the section's quoted guidance-and-ease pair in 92:12, this ayah warns of a blazing Fire, continuing the path's consequence into the same destination named in Surah 87.
The section names root ش ق و for the wretched traveler; this continuation says that only the most wretched will enter the Fire, joining the root's hardship sense to the wrong destination.
The section says the worst person turns aside from the reminder; this ayah describes the Fire-bound person as one who denies and turns away, specifying that refusal in the same surah.
The section's root ج ن ب describes keeping the reminder aside; here the most God-fearing is kept away from the Fire, reversing the wretched person's direction in 92:16.
The section's wider surah calls successful the one who purifies himself; this continuation describes the giver who spends wealth to purify himself, linking the easy course to purification.
The section identifies the giver as one set on the easier course; this ayah clarifies that his giving is not repayment of a favor owed to anyone.
The section frames the course as a journey under divine guidance; this ayah gives the giver's aim as seeking his Lord's face, specifying the journey's orientation.
The section contrasts easy and hard courses; this closing ayah says the giver will be satisfied, completing the easier course's promised end.
The section cites 92:12 on guidance; this next ayah places both the first life and the Hereafter with God, setting the temporal frame for the fire and deliverance in 92:14–21.
The section says the fearful remember while the wretched avoid the reminder; this ayah calls the revelation itself a reminder, immediately after the fleeing-animal image in 74:49–51.
The section distinguishes the one who remembers from the one who turns aside; this neighboring ayah says whoever wills may remember, stating the hearer's choice after 74:54.
The section names root ه د ي for showing a road and dictionary form سَوَاءٌ for an even way; traveling toward Midian, Moses asks his Lord to guide him to a sound way.
The section names root ه د ي for guidance and develops a route made easy; this ayah tells Moses to make a dry path through the sea and promises the travelers will not fear pursuit.
The section says the course taken determines its outcome; this ayah shows Pharaoh and his troops pursuing the sea path and being overwhelmed, completing 20:77's safe crossing with the pursuers' fate.
The section's root ه د ي names the guide who leads forward; this ayah says Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them, explaining the failed pursuit in 20:78.
The section gives a guided route with different responses; this ayah sets up Moses' sea crossing when his companions fear that the pursuing force will overtake them.
The section names root ه د ي for guidance; facing capture at the sea, Moses says his Lord is with him and will guide him, making the guide's role a concrete deliverance.
The section develops passage over a difficult route; this ayah has Moses strike the sea and God split it, making a traversable way for the people in 26:61–62.
The section distinguishes travelers by how they take a route; this ayah brings the pursuing force to the crossing too, placing both groups at the same passage before their different ends.
The section connects guidance to the safer course; this ayah says Moses and those with him were saved together, giving the guided group's outcome in the sea crossing.
The section contrasts the wretched traveler's end with the guided way; this ayah says the pursuing group was drowned, completing the opposite outcome to 26:65.

The section names root ه د ي for guidance and pairs ease with difficulty; this ayah describes guidance as an opened heart and misguidance as constriction like climbing into the sky, joining direction to felt ease or strain.

The section develops a route and the remembrance that distinguishes its traveler; this ayah names the Lord's straight path and says its signs are made clear for people who remember, continuing 6:125's guidance contrast.
The section cites the steep pass in 90:11; this earlier ayah says the human was created in hardship, giving the ascent's difficulty a human setting in the same passage.
The section's image asks how a traveler is guided along a road; this ayah asks where people are going, framing the direction question that verses 27–29 answer.
The section's 87:9–11 passage distinguishes responses to a reminder; this ayah identifies the revelation as a reminder for all worlds, answering the question in 81:26.
The section joins the route to a traveler's response; this ayah says the reminder is for whoever wills to be upright, identifying the direction at stake after 81:27.
The section's route involves human response under divine guidance; this ayah qualifies the hearer's willing by God's will, completing the choice sequence in 81:26–28.
The section says the wretched person turns aside from the reminder; this ayah describes someone who is reminded of God's signs and turns away, then says he will not be guided when called to guidance.

The section says the fearful remember when reminded; this ayah says only the one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen can be warned, joining fear, following, and reminder in one description.

The section says the one who fears remembers; this ayah describes God's revealed message moving those who fear Him from trembling to softened hearts and remembrance, giving a specific response to the reminder.

The section's wider surah contrasts preferring worldly life with the lasting Hereafter; this ayah describes the one who wants the immediate life and assigns Hell as his outcome, setting up 17:19's opposite course.
The section contrasts the nearer life with the better, lasting Hereafter; this ayah describes the believer who seeks the Hereafter and strives for it, the other course to 17:18.
The section's wider surah says people prefer worldly life; this ayah says people love the immediate life, stating the same orientation before 75:21 names what they leave.
The section contrasts the nearer life with the more lasting Hereafter; this ayah says people leave the Hereafter, completing the preference in 75:20.
The section names root ه د ي for guidance and contrasts the one who follows it with the one who turns aside; this ayah says Thamud preferred blindness to guidance and were seized by punishment.

The section's root ه د ي also has a dictionary sense of a weak, swaying walker supported by two people; this ayah says human beings are weak and God wants to lighten their burden, a thematic echo rather than a walking scene.
